description: Why three encoders make three file sizes from one photo, explained at the pace of an MSN chat. AVIF vs JPEG vs jpegli, with a bytes-per-pixel demo that fetches the real encoded files live.
composeNote: This is a recorded conversation. The demo above measures real files.
disclosure: Starter draft. This grew out of the garage encoding study, where one photo runs through every encoder and the bytes get counted. The conversation is a first pass; the demo fetches the study's real output files and measures their actual sizes.

editorial.reader: A curious reader who knows the surface term but wants the mechanism.
editorial.problem: The reader can recognize encoding vocabulary without being able to predict what its mechanism will do.
editorial.thesis: The page should leave the reader able to explain encoding in plain language and predict its behavior.
evidence: The conversation cites its sources and the demos make the mechanism visible.
The understanding check names common misconceptions and explains every answer.
editorial.uncertainty: The demos teach the model; they do not replace a measurement or a full treatment.

understanding.intro: Before you jump to the garage study: pop quiz, four questions. If the bytes-per-pixel table made sense, this takes a minute.

questions.q: Start from the top. One photo goes through three encoders and comes out at three different sizes. Where does the shrink actually come from?

options.t: it throws away detail my eye would skip anyway, then packs what survives
options.why: That is the whole game. Every lossy encoder discards what you would never notice, fine high-frequency detail and fine color, and the three differ in how cleverly they choose what to drop.

options.t: it scales the image down to fewer pixels and stretches it back up
options.why: All three files keep every one of the 106,400 pixels; the live table divides real bytes by that same pixel count. The savings come from discarding invisible detail while the pixel grid stays put.

options.t: it just zips the bytes harder, like a better rar
options.why: Lossless packing is what PNG does, and the live table shows it losing badly to every lossy format. The lossy three win because they are allowed to throw information away, and an eye model decides what.

options.t: newer formats have better math, so files shrink automatically with age
options.why: Age alone explains little: jpegli writes the 1992 JPEG format and still roughly halves the baseline. The win is in how an encoder spends its bits, which the three-encoder grid shows directly.

questions.q: AVIF measures smallest on the full photo, so why does each thumbnail on this site ship a zenjpeg JPEG as well?

options.t: avif needs a modern decoder, so the jpeg is the fallback anything can read
options.why: Right: AVIF decodes only on recent browsers, so the picture element offers AVIF first and the zenjpeg .jpg catches everything else. Universal but larger against modern but smaller, and each visitor downloads exactly one.

options.t: browsers grab both versions and keep whichever one renders faster
options.why: The picture element commits before downloading: the browser picks the first source it can decode and never fetches the rest. One visitor pays for one file, which is the point of dual-encoding.

options.t: the jpeg is the higher-quality copy, kept around for people who zoom in
options.why: Both tiers target the same visual quality; the JPEG tier just needs more bytes to hit it inside the old format. The fallback exists for decode support, as the 23:04 message lays out.

options.t: avif only wins on tiny crops, so full-size photos still need the jpeg
options.why: Backwards on both ends: the live table shows AVIF winning outright on the full photo, while the 96-pixel zoom crops are where AVIF's fixed container overhead makes it look heavy. Reread the caption under the format grid.

questions.q: In the stripes demo, switching from 4:4:4 to 4:2:0 drops the stored samples to half. What did you actually see change on the canvas?

options.t: the black and white lines stayed sharp, the red-green ones dissolved
options.why: That is chroma subsampling in one picture: luma keeps full resolution and carries the sharpness, while the two chroma planes drop to one sample per 2x2 block. Your eye resolves brightness far better than color, so photos barely show it.

options.t: the whole test card went softer, both bands about equally
options.why: Only the color band pays. Flip the demo again: the luma stripes hold razor sharp at every mode, because subsampling shrinks the two chroma planes and leaves luma at full resolution.

options.t: the colors washed out toward gray but kept their crisp edges
options.why: The 2x2 averaging blends neighboring red and green stripes into mud, so the color detail loses exactly its edges; edges survive only in the untouched luma plane. Toggle 4:2:0 and study the bottom band.

options.t: the picture dimmed a little, since half the samples are gone
options.why: Brightness survives untouched because every discarded sample is chroma. The 4:2:0 file keeps full luma plus quarter-resolution color, which is why the info line reads 50% of raw samples with zero visible dimming.

questions.q: Last one. jpegli writes the same JPEG bitstream as mozjpeg, at the same quality knob, and still measures smallest in the encoder grid. What is its actual edge?

options.t: it models the eye: xyb color, per-block quantization, smarter rounding
options.why: That is the psychovisual win: jpegli spends bits where your eye looks and starves detail you would never see, all while staying a standard JPEG a 1995 decoder reads. Roughly 25% over the old mozjpeg.

options.t: it sneaks avif-style prediction tricks inside the jpeg container
options.why: The bitstream stays plain 1992 JPEG, which is the whole point of the fallback: ancient decoders read it. Larger blocks and sharper prediction are AVIF's tricks, and they require an AV1 decoder.

options.t: it quietly drops to 4:2:0 chroma while mozjpeg keeps full color
options.why: The encoder grid pinned all three to the same settings; subsampling is a separate knob with its own two demos. jpegli's gain comes from where it rounds, per block, tuned to perception.

options.t: it runs a lower quality setting internally, trading sharpness for bytes
options.why: The grid held all three encoders to the same q72 and jpegli still came out smallest at like quality. It aims its bits more accurately instead of spending fewer bits on a worse picture.

messages.html: the garage page runs one photo through jpeg, jpegli, and avif and prints three different sizes. before I trust those numbers, tell me why one image even gives three sizes.

An encoder throws away the detail your eye skips, then packs what survives. The three differ in how hard they push each step.

JPEG (1992) cuts the photo into 8x8 blocks, runs a cosine transform, and rounds off the high-frequency parts. jpegli (Google, 2024) keeps the exact JPEG format but rounds smarter, so it fits roughly 25% more quality into the same bytes as the old mozjpeg encoder. AVIF borrows AV1's video tricks, larger blocks and sharper prediction, so it usually wins on bytes-per-pixel outright.
so jpegli writes a normal .jpg that any browser opens, just smaller?

Right. jpegli stays inside the JPEG bitstream, so a browser from 1995 still decodes it. AVIF needs a modern decoder (Safari 16+, Chrome 85+). That trade, universal but larger against modern but smaller, is why the photo grid ships both and lets the browser pick.
ok, stop describing it. show me the bytes on one photo.

demo.html:
The same 400×266 photo (106,400 pixels), run through every encoder. These sizes are fetched live from the files the garage study actually produced, so the bytes are real. The last column is size against the lossless PNG.

messages.html: so on this photo jpegli is about half the baseline JPEG, and avif is smaller still. what's the catch with avif then?

Decode support and encode time. AVIF leans on the AV1 codec, which is slower to encode and only decodes on recent browsers. jpegli is fast and universal. That is why the site builds jpegli from source for the universal fallback and uses AVIF as the primary <picture> source: the browser reaches for AVIF, and anything that cannot decode it falls back to the jpegli .jpg.
and the grayscale shots? why are those so much smaller?

A color image carries one luma plane (brightness) plus two chroma planes (color). Drop to grayscale and you delete both chroma planes, roughly two-thirds of the color information, so the file falls hard. The garage study has the side-by-side counts.
so color is two of the three planes. JPEG and AVIF don't even keep color at full resolution, right? that's the subsampling thing?

Right, chroma subsampling. Your eye resolves brightness far better than color, so codecs keep luma at full resolution and shrink the two chroma planes. 4:4:4 keeps everything; 4:2:2 halves chroma horizontally; 4:2:0, the web default, stores one chroma sample per 2x2 block, a quarter of the color resolution. The luma carries the sharpness, so you barely notice.

demo.html: The top band is fine luma detail (black and white lines); the bottom is fine chroma detail (red and green lines) at the same spacing. Switch the mode: luma stays razor sharp at every setting, while the color detail dissolves as you drop chroma resolution.

messages.html: wild, the black-and-white lines stay razor sharp at 4:2:0 but the red-green lines just dissolve. and that's half the samples gone.

Exactly, and for photographs it is almost free, because real scenes rarely put fine high-contrast color edges right next to each other. Where it shows is red text on a dark background or saturated line art, which is why screenshots and graphics keep 4:4:4 while photos ship 4:2:0.
earlier you said jpegli just "rounds smarter." smarter how, if it writes the same JPEG format?

It models your eye instead of trusting the fixed 1992 quantization tables. jpegli works in the XYB color space, which spaces colors the way you perceive them, sets the quantization adaptively per block by what you would actually notice, and rounds with adaptive dead-zones. The output is still a standard JPEG that any decoder reads, but more bits land where your eye looks and fewer on detail you would never see. That is the rough 25% it gains over the old mozjpeg encoder.
ok, I want to SEE these tradeoffs, not just read byte counts. show me one zoomed crop across formats and qualities.
Here is a 96-pixel detail crop, the car's body edge against the dark wheel, run through every encoder and blown up so the artifacts show. Start with format against quality.

demo.html:
One 96-pixel detail crop (the body edge against the dark wheel), run through three formats at three quality tiers and shown pixel-zoomed. Read across a row to compare formats at one quality; read down to watch a format fall apart as quality drops.

highmidlow jpegli WebP AVIF

At 96 pixels the absolute bytes mostly reflect each format's fixed container overhead (WebP's is lightest, AVIF's heaviest), not the per-pixel efficiency that flips on full images, which is what the live measurement above shows. What the zoom reveals is the artifact style: JPEG breaks into 8x8 blocks, while WebP and AVIF smear and smudge instead.

messages.html: jpeg goes blocky, the others go smeary. now the jpeg encoders you mentioned, mozjpeg vs the google one?
Same crop, same quality knob, three encoders. The bytes under each tell the story.

demo.html:
The same crop, the same quality setting (q72), three JPEG encoders. All three write the same JPEG format any decoder reads; the only difference is how cleverly each spends its bits. Watch the byte counts.

Same quality knob, real bytes measured live: jpegli comes out smallest, well under both mozjpeg and the system baseline, because it models your eye (XYB color, adaptive per-block quantization) and stops spending bits on detail you would not notice. That is the psychovisual win in one crop.

messages.html: jpegli really is smaller at the same setting. and chroma, up close on a real edge?
The same crop as a JPEG at the three chroma samplings. Luma holds; the color is what softens.

demo.html:
Chroma subsampling on a real edge instead of stripes: the same crop saved as a JPEG at 4:4:4, 4:2:2, and 4:2:0. The luma edge holds at every setting; the color is what loses resolution.

The size drop is modest here (4:4:4 to 4:2:0) because this crop is mostly grays. On saturated content the savings grow and the color fringing gets obvious, which is the stark version in the stripes demo above.

messages.html: so what does the site actually ship per thumbnail?

Each thumbnail is dual-encoded: an AVIF primary and a zenjpeg JPEG fallback inside one <picture>, plus a 400px AVIF tier for phones. The browser loads the smallest format it can decode and never downloads the others.
